Here's where **Plastic pathways** (#2) stands, with the most relevant new papers and a funding suggestion.

## Where the project stands

I can see the project's members — Jonah Whitcombe, Priya Raman, and you — but its confirmed state (goals, method, blockers, milestones) is empty in Mycelium, so I can't say how far along the work is. If that's out of date, you can update it in the app.

Its current slate has ten items, all entered this week (10–13 Nov).

## Three most relevant new papers

1. **#4 — "A tide-resolving beaching kernel for marine litter"** (Lim & Hong, 2026). The closest match: a three-phase beaching kernel plus six particle kernels for OceanParcels 3.1.4, validated against field records from Uido, Korea, using ROMS flow fields. Directly usable for modelling where floating debris ends up.
2. **#9 — "A Deep Learning Framework for Automatic Detection and Segmentation of Internal Solitary Waves in Satellite Imagery"** (Rong et al., 2026). Not about plastic, but a strong methodological template: YOLO11-based detection and pixel-level segmentation of low-contrast, curved features in MODIS imagery, applied over a decade of data. The same approach could be turned toward detecting debris or surface films from space.
3. **#5 — "Daily Analyses of the Pacific Regional Ocean Forecast System model"** (Zhang, 2026). A Zenodo deposit of daily analyses of a regional ocean forecast system — relevant as a workflow for running and checking the kind of flow fields particle tracking depends on. (I could only see its title and metadata, so I'm flagging it as the weakest of the three.)

The other slate items — #3, #11 (phytoplankton production), #7 (a comment), #8 (multi-object tracking) — are further from the project's core.

## One funding opportunity

**#6 — NSF Ocean Technology and Interdisciplinary Coordination (OTIC)**, deadline 15 Feb 2027, still open. It supports unsolicited proposals for instrumentation and technology development with broad applicability to ocean science. The strongest fit: the #4 beaching kernel is exactly the kind of reusable, broadly applicable tool OTIC funds, and it sits squarely in the lab's declared "debris pathways" cluster. The biggest doubt: OTIC leans toward hardware and instrumentation, so a purely software/kernel proposal would need to be framed as a capability that enhances observational or analytical practice more widely.

If you'd like, I can dig into the full text of #4 or #9, or check what's in the project's saved items.
